<reason>Both sides delivered a high-level economic debate, but Side B won by proving more rigorous on the financing and balance-of-payments mechanics in the second half. While Side A effectively argued that importing basic essentials is a recurring foreign-exchange leak, Side B successfully exposed a fatal gap in Side A's transition plan: regional factories still require continuous hard-currency imports (machinery, spare parts, chemical precursors, and grid turbines) while earning local currencies, and extractive revenues cannot effortlessly stay flat if all new infrastructure and credit are diverted elsewhere. Side B also gave stronger answers to the Pressure Questions—including turning the technological obsolescence argument by showing specialized battery plants risk stranding faster than raw copper or gas—while Side A had a minor word-limit clip in Rebuttal 1 and left Side B's Rebuttal 2 critiques of mine depletion and ongoing input imports largely unanswered in Closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In Rebuttal 2 (B4.2–B4.4), Side B flipped Side A's technology-risk question by showing that shifts in battery chemistry strand costly domestic battery factories while copper, gas, and dual-use rail/power retain value, and simultaneously dismantled Side A's claim that existing mines can keep funding the transition without new capital or infrastructure upgrades.</best_rebuttal>
